questions.question: Athenian democracy let citizens vote directly on laws. How were most public officials chosen?
options: By appointment from the ten elected generals
By election, with candidates campaigning for votes
By lottery, on the principle that anyone could serve
By inheritance within a handful of old families
questions.answer: By lottery, on the principle that anyone could serve
questions.explanation: Most Athenian offices were filled by sortition, random selection from eligible citizens, because election was considered aristocratic: it favours the wealthy and well-known. Only roles needing specific expertise, notably the ten generals, were elected. Officials served short terms and faced audit afterward. The system rested on the belief that ordinary citizens were competent to govern, which is close to the opposite of what modern democracies assume.
questions.memory_hook: Athens filled most offices by lottery, not election, because they thought voting favoured the rich and famous. Only jobs needing real expertise, like the generals, were elected. Short terms, audits afterward. They assumed ordinary people could govern, which is nearly the reverse of how we do it.

questions.question: Stalingrad (1942-43) is widely called the turning point of the war in Europe. How did the German position collapse?
options: Allied bombing wiped out the German supply depots
Mass defections among Romanian and Italian troops
A Soviet counterattack encircled them from both flanks
A direct assault on the German headquarters in the city
questions.answer: A Soviet counterattack encircled them from both flanks
questions.explanation: Operation Uranus in November 1942 struck the weaker Romanian and Hungarian armies guarding the German flanks rather than the Sixth Army itself, closing a ring around roughly 300,000 men in four days. Hitler forbade a breakout and promised resupply by air, which the Luftwaffe could not deliver. Around 91,000 surrendered in February 1943, and fewer than 6,000 ever came home.
questions.memory_hook: The Soviets did not attack the Germans head-on. Operation Uranus hit the weaker Romanian and Hungarian flanks and closed a ring around 300,000 men in four days. Hitler banned a breakout and promised air resupply that never came. 91,000 surrendered; under 6,000 made it home.

questions.question: William the Conqueror ordered the Domesday Book in 1086, twenty years after the conquest. What was it for?
options: A census of Norman nobles and their new titles
A register of church lands exempt from royal tax
A legal code replacing Anglo-Saxon common law
A survey of who owned what, so it could all be taxed
questions.answer: A survey of who owned what, so it could all be taxed
questions.explanation: Commissioners visited every shire recording landholders, tenants, livestock, ploughs and mills, then sent a second team to verify the first. The detail was unprecedented in medieval Europe and it let the Crown tax accurately and settle ownership disputes left over from the conquest. Contemporaries named it Domesday because, like the Last Judgement, its verdict could not be appealed. It remained legally citable in English courts into the twentieth century.
questions.memory_hook: Commissioners recorded every landholder, tenant, plough and mill in England, then sent a second team to check the first. It let the Crown tax properly and settle conquest-era ownership fights. People called it Domesday because there was no appealing it, like the Last Judgement. Courts still cited it into the 1900s.

questions.question: Jesse Owens and German long jumper Luz Long competed against each other at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. What happened between them?
options: Long was later stripped of his silver for a foul
Long refused to compete and was arrested that night
Long advised Owens on his run-up, then lost to him
Long protested the result and demanded a rematch
questions.answer: Long advised Owens on his run-up, then lost to him
questions.explanation: Owens had fouled twice in qualifying and was close to elimination. Long, his main rival, suggested he move his takeoff mark back to leave margin for error. Owens qualified, went on to win gold, and Long took silver and congratulated him publicly in front of Hitler. They corresponded until Long was killed in Sicily in 1943. Owens later wrote that the friendship meant more to him than the medals.
questions.memory_hook: Owens had two fouls in qualifying and was nearly out. Luz Long, the man he was about to beat, told him to move his takeoff mark back. Owens qualified and won gold; Long took silver and congratulated him publicly in front of Hitler. They wrote to each other until Long died in Sicily in 1943.

questions.question: The 1904 St Louis Olympic marathon is considered the strangest ever run. What did the eventual winner receive mid-race?
options: A bicycle escort over the final three miles
A change of shoes and a fresh pair of dry socks
Strychnine and brandy, given to him by his handlers
Twenty minutes of rest inside a medical tent
questions.answer: Strychnine and brandy, given to him by his handlers
questions.explanation: Thomas Hicks was dosed twice with strychnine sulphate mixed with brandy, then a stimulant in small quantities, and finished hallucinating and barely able to walk. He had to be carried off and nearly died. The first man across the line, Fred Lorz, had ridden eleven miles in a car and was disqualified. Only fourteen of thirty-two starters finished, in dust, heat, and with a single water station on the course.
questions.memory_hook: Thomas Hicks was given strychnine and brandy twice by his own handlers, finished hallucinating, and nearly died. The first man to cross had ridden eleven miles in a car and was disqualified. Fourteen of thirty-two finished, in heat and dust, with one water stop on the whole course.

questions.question: Top Gun (1986) produced a real-world effect the US Navy had not planned for. What was it?
options: Civilian flight schools reported a sudden pilot shortage
Navy aviation applications jumped sharply after release
Recruiters were barred from screening it at events
Congress cut the Navy's aviation budget in response
questions.answer: Navy aviation applications jumped sharply after release
questions.explanation: Navy aviation recruitment rose steeply after release, and the service had set up recruiting tables in cinema lobbies in advance. The Pentagon had given extensive cooperation, supplying aircraft and carrier access at favourable rates, in exchange for script approval. It became a template: military cooperation on films is now routinely conditional on script input. The real Topgun school had also been founded for an unglamorous reason, to fix poor US air-combat kill ratios over Vietnam.
questions.memory_hook: Navy applications spiked, and recruiters had already set up tables in cinema lobbies. The Pentagon supplied jets and carrier access cheaply in return for script approval, which became the template for military film cooperation. The actual Topgun school existed because US kill ratios over Vietnam were bad.

questions.question: Stevie Wonder renegotiated his Motown contract at twenty-one, which almost nobody managed. What did he win?
options: A guaranteed number of singles released every year
A share of Motown's profits across its whole roster
Full creative control and ownership of his publishing
The right to produce records for other Motown artists
questions.answer: Full creative control and ownership of his publishing
questions.explanation: Motown ran a tightly controlled system where staff writers and producers made the creative decisions. Wonder let his contract lapse on his twenty-first birthday, funded independent recordings himself, and returned holding the masters, forcing Berry Gordy to concede artistic control and publishing rights. What followed was Music of My Mind, Talking Book, Innervisions and Songs in the Key of Life, one of the strongest runs in recorded music.
questions.memory_hook: Motown normally decided everything. Wonder let his contract lapse at twenty-one, paid for his own recordings, then came back holding the tapes and made Gordy give him creative control and his publishing. Music of My Mind, Talking Book, Innervisions and Songs in the Key of Life followed.

questions.question: Michelangelo spent four years on the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-1512). What's the popular myth about how he painted it?
options: He used a projector he invented to scale up the designs
He worked 18 months without a break, in total isolation
He stood on scaffolding craning his neck, not lying down
He lay on his back on a specially built curved bed
questions.answer: He stood on scaffolding craning his neck, not lying down
questions.explanation: The 'lying on his back' story comes largely from film and popular retelling. Michelangelo designed his own wooden scaffolding system — a flat platform suspended near the ceiling rather than the arch-based system the Pope's architect suggested. He stood on it and bent backward, working in wet plaster (true fresco) section by section. He wrote a sonnet complaining about his aching neck, curved spine, and deteriorating eyesight. He painted nearly all 5,000 square feet with minimal assistants — mainly for grinding pigments and plastering. The ceiling includes 300+ figures and nine central scenes from Genesis including the iconic Creation of Adam.
questions.memory_hook: Michelangelo wrote a complaining sonnet about his bent spine and ruined eyesight from tilting his head back for four years. He designed custom scaffolding himself. The 'on his back' image is Hollywood — he stood and craned his neck. He painted 5,000 square feet in wet plaster with almost no assistants, including 300+ figures in four years.

questions.question: Antarctica counts as a desert even though it holds most of the planet's fresh water. What qualifies it?
options: Its surface has no soil that could support plants
Deserts are defined by temperature, not rainfall
Its water is locked as ice and so does not count
It gets less precipitation than the Sahara does
questions.answer: It gets less precipitation than the Sahara does
questions.explanation: A desert is defined by precipitation, not heat: under roughly 250mm a year. The Antarctic interior receives about 50mm, less than the Sahara, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys may have had no rain for two million years. The ice sheet is thick because almost nothing melts, so tiny annual snowfalls accumulate over hundreds of thousands of years. Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth by area.
questions.memory_hook: Deserts are about rainfall, not heat. The Antarctic interior gets around 50mm a year, less than the Sahara, and the Dry Valleys may not have seen rain in two million years. The ice is thick because nothing melts, so tiny snowfalls pile up over millennia. It is the biggest desert on Earth.

questions.question: Table salt dissolves in water because it is held together by ionic bonds. What is an ion?
options: An atom whose nucleus has started to decay
An atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it has charge
Two atoms sharing a pair of electrons between them
An atom that has gained or lost neutrons, changing its mass
questions.answer: An atom that has gained or lost electrons, so it has charge
questions.explanation: Sodium gives up an electron and becomes positive; chlorine takes one and becomes negative; the opposite charges hold the crystal together. Water molecules are polar, with slightly charged ends, so they surround and pull the ions apart, which is what dissolving is. Ions in solution conduct electricity, which is why salt water conducts and pure water barely does, and why nerves and muscles depend on ion movement.
questions.memory_hook: Sodium loses an electron and goes positive, chlorine gains one and goes negative, and the attraction holds salt together. Water is polar, so it surrounds the ions and pulls them apart. Free ions carry current, which is why salt water conducts and why your nerves need them.

questions.question: About a third of Socotra's plant species exist nowhere else on Earth. What explains that?
options: Medieval traders deliberately planted the species there
It split from the mainland roughly 20 million years ago
Monsoon winds cut it off for half of every year
Its soil chemistry kills off most introduced species
questions.answer: It split from the mainland roughly 20 million years ago
questions.explanation: Socotra separated from the Arabian mainland roughly 20 million years ago and its flora evolved in isolation, producing the dragon blood tree with its inverted-umbrella crown and the bulbous desert rose. About 37% of its 830 vascular plant species are endemic, a higher rate than the Galapagos at around 30%. The island is arid and was never intensively farmed, so much survived. Goats, road building and conflict in Yemen now threaten it.
questions.memory_hook: Socotra broke off the Arabian mainland about 20 million years ago and its plants evolved alone, which is where the dragon blood tree and the bottle-trunk desert rose came from. Around 37% of its 830 plant species exist nowhere else, beating the Galapagos at roughly 30%. Goats and Yemen's war are the current threat.

sources.claim: 37% of Socotra's 830 vascular plant species endemic; Galapagos ~30%

questions.question: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, yet one is the hardest natural substance and the other flakes apart in your fingers. Why?
options: The atoms are bonded in completely different arrangements
Diamond contains trace nitrogen that hardens the structure
Graphite is carbon mixed with a small amount of clay
Diamond forms under pressure and graphite under heat
questions.answer: The atoms are bonded in completely different arrangements
questions.explanation: In diamond every carbon atom bonds to four others in a rigid three-dimensional lattice, so there is no easy plane along which it can fail. Graphite bonds each atom to three others in flat sheets, with only weak forces between sheets, so the layers slide, which is why pencils work and why graphite lubricates. Same element, different geometry, opposite properties. Graphite is actually the more stable form at room temperature, so diamonds are very slowly turning into it.
questions.memory_hook: Diamond bonds each carbon to four neighbours in a rigid 3D lattice with no weak plane. Graphite bonds three, making flat sheets held together loosely, so the layers slide, which is how pencils write. Same atom, different geometry. Graphite is the stabler form, so diamonds are slowly becoming it.
